projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Malcolm McDonald was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Okay. I'm Candice Nunnally and I'm interviewing someone from World War II.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Okay. My name is Malcolm McDonald, originally from Minnesota. I signed up for the Army in July '42 in the Reserves because I was gonna be drafted. I was called out to duty August 1, 1942. I want to Camp Curry, Ohio for six weeks. Then down to Fort Polk for about four months. We had desert training -- not desert training, but fire maneuver and all kinds of basic down there and in the, like, say, the swamps of Louisiana. Tank training and firing with the 11th armored division.

We were there about two years and then we went to Camp Barkeley, Texas for further training. Then up to Camp Ibis, which is the Mojave Big Desert, which is now the desert training center, which is Camp Irwin, California. We stayed there about a for about a year and a half, two years. Oh, possibly, a year and a half. And we all got our equipment and then we went to Camp -- what is -- Camp Roberts, California. And they didn't have room for us, they didn't need us. So we went to, what they call, another camp, which is now Vandenberg Air Force Base, Camp Roberts.

From there we got on a train and road all the way to Brooklyn Army Terminal and got on a ship and went to Europe. This was in August of '43. We went to England and we were in staging area in England for quite a few years. And we did not make the invasion, but we landed about six weeks after the invasion of June 6, 1944. We landed Cherbourg, went on in, followed the same route through France, and we were gonna head down to Southern Germany and take care of Austria and Czechoslovakia and all the troops down there. And we got sudden call to travel 350 miles north, go to the Battle of the Bulge. So we had to turn our tanks around and go day and night for three or four days to get up to the Battle of the Bulge which is in December 1944.

So we all get credit for the Battle of the Bulge which lasted about six weeks. Seemed like six months. The snow and the cold and after that they divided us up. We were in Patton's Third Army by that time. Then Patton took over his original duty down in southern Germany and they shipped us down in there and ended up in Linz, Austria which is on the Danube River. And before that we freed Mauthausen Concentration Camp which is right outside of Linz near Munich.

We also went to Dachau. So when we got to Linz, the Russians were on one side of the river and we were on the other side, and we didn't want to cross the river in their territory. We didn't like them, they didn't like us. And we were really afraid of each other because we didn't want to step on their territory and we didn't want them in our territory. So after that well we just, kind of, phased on out, changed units, and they had the, you might say, the evacuation and we had to go around and go through the houses, collect all the weapons, see what men were there, and gather up prisoners and any stray people.

Then the Military Government took over and from there on it was peace and tranquility and they sent us back for staging area for the trip home. So you have any questions that I can help you with? It's not -- it's kind of a brief summary but its so long ago I can't remember it all.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: That was -- that was good. So after the war were you allowed in any another kind of military?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: After the war? Oh, yeah. Oh, yes. After the war I came back and -- I came back in February '46. I got married in '47. And I stayed in Reserve, Minnesota National Guard and Reserve. And I'll be darned if I didn't get called up for the Korean War. So what happened? I end up back in the Army for the Korean War. Went to Korea in August of 1950. I spent the winter of '50 and '51. Came home January '52, which was really colder winter in Korea than it was in Germany. I guess we were moving so fast, but Korea was a terrible experience with the people and the roads and the sanitation. And more or less the living conditions in the mountains not near the source and near the sea and living in the field and sleeping on the ground is really worse than Germany, I think. That's the worst time I ever had. So you got so many points. It was a 16 months tour and you got credit for any combat tours you had over there. You got three points for every month you were in combat and I had three months. So I had extra points but I still didn't get home any earlier. Somebody lost it. They lost the count of my credits so -- You're not on the front line all the time. You're some back in reserve, sometime on the front lines, and you're in, you're out, you're here, you're there. And actually like everything else, it's a big blur because you don't know where you are. You never were there before. And you never -- you don't have a map so you really don't know what's going on 'til it's all over with. Then you get back and read about it in the paper or see it in the newsreel. It's really -- then you could study, oh, that's what happened. Here we are. That's where they were. We were here and you were there. And this was going on over there.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Did you have any close friends in the war?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Did I have what? What?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Like, any close friends or anybody?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: I had a couple of men that -- in are unit that were killed on guard duty unexpectedly, naturally. They were guarding the perimeter in Belgium and troops came up and naturally fired at them. And they disappeared. And one of our own buddies was shot by our own people because in the dark you don't know who anybody is and you hear somebody over there --

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: And he got there first and he, unfortunately, called friendly fire and they didn't call a friendly fire then. It was just an unavoidable accident. But that's one of my friends got shot that way -- by his own people. We also had ring mobs on all are equipment, naturally, and shooting and crossfire there. And lots of time we didn't know what we hit. Ya know? Far away and in the dark.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Okay. There was nothing glamorous about it. You just, kind of, put up with it and went along your way and did what you could.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: At the times of the war, how do you feel about it?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: The times of the war?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well we're young and excited and we're all, more or less, proud to be in the Army and proud to serve our country and be over there. If some of your buddies back home were 4-Fs and didn't go they felt terrible about it. So it was a time when there was high spirit, high moral, and the country was behind their president and the people. And everybody agreed with their Congress and the Congress was behind the Army. And there was no exceptions. This is the rule. This is what it is. And that's the way it is for everybody. And we found out later there was a few exceptions; but, on the whole though, everybody is treated very fair and did their part and nobody bothered you.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Did you all have lots of supplies? Or did --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, well, as far as supplies, we -- during the Battle of the Bulge we run short on gasoline and food because we traveled so far, so fast in that short period of time that they -- they couldn't get the food and gasoline up to us cause the tanks and we got about, oh at that time, four to six miles to the gallon of gas in these Sherman tanks we had. And they formed the Red Ball Express down and near the ports. Le Havre and the other ports along the French coast formed the Red Ball Express, which was convoys of maybe 30-40 two-and-a-half ton trucks loaded with five-gallon cans of gasoline. They would go steady, go through any town, empty, secure the road, get any thing out the road, and they would buzz on through, and the only thing that had the same priority would be ammunitions and shells for the front lines, and then they'd refuel the tanks and go on again. And they had the same problem going back. They'd take 'em as long to go back and they'd have to load up again and go back and catch and they didn't have any of the tankers that they have now. And the Air Force couldn't get through because there was so many clouds, the fog, rain, and mist and snow -- the weather was real bad so -- it was bad for traveling, air, and for driving.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: During the war did y'all do anything to entertain yourselves? Was there anywhere to go or I don't know. Did you just --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well, the only time we'd stop and get a rest period we had have to do our laundry. And we spent our time playing cards and sleeping, catching up on our rest. Once in a while, every, maybe six weeks, two or three months, a shower and laundry unit would come through and have outside showers with canvas around it and a pipe and a shower head and a water truck. And they'd spray some water on you, give you a shower and you throw your clothes in one pile, go through the shower and come out and you get some fresh clothes on your way out. And all that time your freezing to death. But about every two to three months you need a shower anyhow that's for sure. (Laughter)

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: (Laughter) (Phone Ringing)

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Ah, I'll just let it ring. Wife's upstairs.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Okay. Are you in any organizations now? (Phone Ringing)

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I belong to the American Legion Post 284 - Colonial Heights and Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 2239 - Colonial Heights out in 301. And I belong to the Retired Military Association and to the Association of Members of the Battle of the Bulge. That's about enough.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: What was your rank when you left the --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: All that time I was Staff Sergent in World War II. And when I got out, they called me back in for Korea, I got Tech Sergeant. Then -- I stayed in because I had about 9-11, 10-11 years in. I said well, I'll stay for 20 years. I got 22 years in in the early 60s. I was gonna retire and guess what? Vietnam came along and said your selected retention, you're an engineer, combat engineers are scarce. And I was a War Officer by then. So I couldn't get out. I went to Vietnam in '64 and '65. Come back. Sent me over there '68-'69. I was there for the Tet Offensive, big -- the New Years celebration and Tet Offensive when the VC rolls up and had a sneak attack through every major village or city and they thought they defeated us and they did quite a bit of damage. Burnt half the Saigon down and Qui Nhon and Hue but they didn't beat us. But they did change public opinion and they made a big impression. And we found out later that they had a lot of funerals that summer. And what they were doing was carrying these coffins down these mountains and through the cities and down to the -- on the way to the burial grounds and they weren't coffins; they were loaded with ammunition, warheads, mines, and rifles and they plant them in the ground instead of bodies and at the given signal they would dig 'em up. And kept offensive. At one o'clock in the morning, and that's when they struck about 3 o'clock in the morning, 4 o'clock in the morning, on the Tet Offensive which was in February of 1968. And they did a real good job. You ever hear of the Tet Offensive? Tet is a New Years celebration for over in the far east. They have the year of the horse and the monkey and the snake and the this and the that. And Tet is New Years and they celebrate for about three weeks. And that's when they attacked, during the celebration when the Vietnamese soldiers -- we were on our side, the others were the Viet Cong. We worked with the Vietnamese people and they'd take two hour noon lunch hour. And after the Tet Offensives they didn't take two hour lunch hour. They found out they were at war, so they were on the job. (Laughter)

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: That's about it if you don't have any other --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well, I say, at the time I thought we was going through many tough times, going through hell, but once the experience is over with, you come out okay, it's the experience that you wouldn't give a million dollars to sign up for, but once it's over with you wouldn't give a million dollars not to go through with it because you travel, you see people, you see other countries, and realize how lucky and fortunate we are in this country to have all the freedoms and good living conditions and enjoy the privileges we do in this country.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well, freedom does not come free.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: (Laughter) Where do you end up in Europe last?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: End up down in Linz, Austria, down in the border. Which is -- Hitler went to high school down in Linz, Austria when he was a kid. Yeah, Linz.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: You mentioned some of the concentration camps --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Dachau is outside of Munich and Mauthausen outside of Linz. That was -- this is in the southern part of Germany, you might say. The other concentration camps were further up north in Poland and up in that area. We didn't go in there, that wasn't our area. See there were several armies over there and we were Patton's Third Army. We were responsible for southern Germany.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Was Rommel involved in that Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: No, he was not.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: He was in Africa, wasn't he?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. They had -- Von Rundstedt was the german commander. Rommel was in Africa and then he got relieved and got in trouble with Hitler for something. Of course, he had two or three years of African war over there and he was pretty well beat by that time. And he got sick. I think he had diabetes or cancer of the liver or something. He didn't live too much longer after that. But he wasn't involved in that. He did inspect the front before we landed and set up the defenses though. He engineered the defenses and pill boxes and told Hitler how the defenses should be set up and where the lots for the troops coming in, but he wasn't directly involved with it as far as I know. There were several Panzer divisions that were placed nearby. That's why they had such high casualties when they went in. And Hitler held back three other Panzer divisions and wouldn't let them go because he thought that was a false invasion and he thought that they were gonna -- invite -- invade from southern France and southern Italy and they had a dummy force down there with these, oh, tanks, guns, and artillery pieces blowed up made artificially like a movie for staging area and they took pictures and when we flew over the area thought we were gonna invade southern France and Italy and that was the dummy part and we were coming in off of Cherbourg and Calais and up in that way. So Hitler out -- he had a chance to wipe us out, but he held back three armored divisions until it was too late and it didn't do any good. We got in, got all our equipment landed and got in, which we were in about the third phase. We were in reserves in the armored division at that time. Ninth, tenth, and eleventh were Patton's Third Army. And we come in last because they didn't even know where they were gonna need us, see? And then we ended up, started south and then changed it and we went north up to the Battle of the Bulge. Up in Belgium, Laage, Luxembourg up in that area, Laage. In fact, I had some maps and my book on the history of the whole thing and it's been so long, I haven't seen 'em and I can't find 'em. I don't know where they are. I was gonna have this book for you and all. I do have some French maps here I can show you but these were actually our history and our trail. But I asked the wife and she had I haven't seen that for 20 years. (Laughter) Well, I don't know where it was either. Really, I'm amazed. I said, well how can we get that? Up in the attic, down in the garage? And I'm sorry I couldn't find it.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Oh, it's okay.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: That would be a graphic picture of the whole history. It's about that thick. And before we come home, they want us to write this up and submit it and everybody got a copy of it.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: How old were you when you joined?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: I was 19 when I went in.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. I had three and a half -- 3 years, 8 months, and 28 days in World War II. And then I had almost three years in Korea. And, at that time, they called me back again for my job up there so I'll stay. And then they come on with Vietnam. Here I am, thirty year man.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Did you stay 30 years?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. 31.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. But the last few years were with good duty. Because the higher in rank you go, the better job you get and you get in the headquarters in group and brigade and battal. I ended in Engineer Command Headquarters last time I was there, see? You know, the advisors, the colonels, the inspector. You know, you do, more or less, consulting and trouble shooting and, more or less, go to meetings and they talk about it and decide what planning -- a lot of planning, see? That's the nice part.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Sounds good.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. But I'm glad it's over with.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Oh. I bet that. What kind of sniper did you have?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: It was a -- I think, it was a Sherman. We had the M4 A4. I remember that part. I think it was a Sherman. It only had a 75 milammeter gun when we first went in. And after we were there at the Battle of the Bulge, just before it was changing over to the 90 milammeter because these German tanks were shooting at us out of range. We'd shoot with ours and would land maybe three or four blocks short and they could out shoot us, the other range. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah, have to stay out of range.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Well the German eighty-eight Acht-Anoxic(PH), that's what it was, Acht-Anoxie(PH) eighty-eight German, that was anti-aircraft, anti-personal, anti-tank weapon. Yeah. It would go right through our --- his armor, make a whole that big on one side. Go right on through, you could look through.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: That's right. And naturally, yeah. And the armor on the side wasn't as thick as the -- and it would go through that. But when it went through it would explode all the ammunition in there and gasoline, naturally the tanks would spring a leak and the sparks and the heat, end up with the burnt up tank.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Was the inside of the tanks painted white?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah, I remember.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: There all painted white, yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Inside a hundred percent enamel?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. White enamel. There like the inside of a refrigerator.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Mm-Hmm.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. For sanitation and good vision.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah, I was gonna ask what was the reason.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. That's for good visibility and for sanitation to keep us clean.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Awfully dark in there when the hatch is closed, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, oh yeah. Oh, you got little pilot lights though and that helped reflect the light, you know? Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: How much gasoline would one of those tanks hold? 50 gallons? 20 gallons?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, no. They held up to 180, come to my mind. Oh, yeah. Somewhere in that.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: They have to have a pretty big capacity?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: You get four or five miles to the gallon?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: 180 gallons is --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: You can't stop at every corner and get a, you know, a refill.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: You get fifty miles almost.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, something like that.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: 90 miles on 5 miles to the gallon.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: (5 second ___)That's pretty good capacity at that time. Did you have to pre-crank the engines before you started them when they were cold?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: We had what we call the little home light starter inside.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, to warm them up and crank them, yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: The reason I was asking is when I was in Fort Hood we had some tanks from the second war.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: When you go out in the morning, you had have to get that long crank and put in there and have to crank that thing about eight times before you could start it.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Did you have a diesel engine? Because we first came out for training, they had diesel engines and you had to crank them. Then they come out with the light tank, the M5, it had twin Cadillac engine with one transfer case. That was the light tank. Cause they couldn't make enough engines of one type to satisfy all sizes and all tanks.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: So here we are with twin Cadillac engine, one transfer case -- I went to tank school. I learned how automatic transmissions work. Style, body, shifting and all that. I went to a couple tank schools, yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: I don't know a lot about that. I do know that the gas -- we had to crank them before.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: We ended up with a 500 horsepower aluminum engine engine in the end. Which 500 horsepower -- well, that's fifty years ago -- that was a lot of power. They got these cars on the road now that got 3-and-400 and these race cars, you know. So, you know, man, 500 horsepower.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Back then --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, it was really something. Yeah. Yeah. Of course, they had several engines. We had diesel engines. We had ___and radio engines in some tanks. Radio engines. 9 cylinder. 7 cylinder. Because, see, they could not make enough engines for one tank to satisfy the whole army.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: So, man, you had to be a genius to keep the thing running. Of course, we had crews to service them too, you know? But as far as the food, there was C-rations and K-rations, by the way. Box -- K-rations are like Cracker Jacks; you open up and eat 'em. And C-rations are can food. Stand for -- acronym for can; C-ration. Beef stew and ham and cheese and ham and eggs and beans.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: They were in cans?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Pork and beans, yeah. And there's a lot of preservatives and they seem like you're eating half preservatives and half food. And then free cigarettes, a lot of chocolate bars. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: A lot of chocolate and a lot of mean cigarettes.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Lots of chesterfields. Nobody liked chesterfield.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: They did not smoke in a car load.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: That's why they gave them away.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Do you remember what it was like arriving when you first got in Europe?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, when I first got in Europe, oh, England was fun, yeah it was nice. Everybody was so friendly. And we train all day and then go out and get a fish and chips at night. And look for a place to have a beer, it was warm beer. And everybody's so friendly with us and a lot -- most of their troops had left and only ones that hadn't left were the guys who didn't know they were gonna go, so you went out to have a good time. And there was always the Red Cross and units have dances and you had fun while you could and it was nice. It was -- we hated to leave England and France after that. It was miserable after that. It was cold and rainy and Battle of the Bulge and so on and so forth. And no time for nothing. You know, just work, work, work, work. You didn't know what day it was and you hardly knew what time it was; didn't matter if it was Saturday, Sunday, holiday. You lose track of everything. I brought back a couple old Yank newspapers, which was an army newspaper. And then there's the Stars and Stripes came out later. Stars and Stripes published over there by somebody in Paris, which was an army newspaper tells what's going on. You can read about what happened last month, you know, or last week.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Well, I would imagine that the Battle of the Bulge was probably the worst path that you saw.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, the Battle of the Bulge was the worst, yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Cold, freezing?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Freezing cold, miserable.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Nothing to eat?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Isolated, didn't know what was going on. Confusion. In fact, in going in through Belgium, they dropped paratroops off. German paratroops dropped off in American uniforms and they had MP armbands on, they changed all the road signs. Tell you, you know -- -we'd come through and say, "Well I'm here, oh, here it is." Neufchâteau you go this way and Luxemburg you go that way. And here we are guided by Germans in American uniforms heading us the wrong way. You know, we found out later that that's how smart they were. That took a lot of guts to do that in enemy territory. So, you know, things like that that at the time it happens, you don't know it, see?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Of course we went by the -- you heard of the Malmedy murder?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Mm-Hmm.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: When all those -- I think it was about 60 or 80 or so troops lined up along side the road in the snow and were massacred. We went right by that. They day after it happened. There was a piece in some paper talking about it, the other day I was reading about it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: I saw a thing on TV --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: On the History Channel --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Where the German's were retreating and they had the prisoners and they couldn't take 'em, so they --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Didn't have room for 'em. Couldn't take 'em. They were losing and they lost all their vehicles and they couldn't feed 'em. Didn't have nobody to guard 'em, so they machined em. Had 'em lined up in rows, along here the road. And they all lined up here and they just opened up the back of the truck and machined 'em. The whole bunch. A couple of them fell down first and bodies fell on top and they lived through it, to talk about it. Snow, oh, about that deep. So, you know, you just take your chances, do the best you can. And, you can't, you know -- it's not -- it's just luck. You gotta be lucky and be in the right place at the right time or in the wrong place at the wrong time. And, you know, some people come out lucky like me, I guess, which thank the Lord. He's watching me all the time; Korea and Vietnam, I guess. Thank the Lord. So anything else you need to know or like to know? It's so long ago that, you know, things are kind-of fuzzy.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Especially, I couldn't find my references. I didn't find them. We changed commanding General's out real quick, too because, you know, I couldn't even name my General in 11th armored division. I was there -- oh, they'd lose Generals and then Generals would make decisions and then direct the -- well, they had have a lot of their harbor officers do duties they didn't like and not to cause any hardship and cross -- you know, well hey, I don't like that guy, he made me do this, he made me do that -- was the best thing to do. They just transfer the General and you get another one to come in, then they start all over, everybody's even. Nobody can say their treated unfair that way, you see?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Start with a new slate. You know what I mean? It's a -- and a -- otherwise, we knew we never -- when you're a Sergeant you don't deal with Generals anyhow, not on our level. So I cant, you know -- they had their staff. And then they have their staff in each battalion and group and regiment and when you get down to a little oh, trooper, I was an accompany, you know, what the heck. I think I was a Sr. General once or twice but I couldn't name my commanding General in our outfit. We did have a General Clark in the states. And I just wonder if it's his father this -- I knew his father -- this Wesley Clark -- I think it was his father that was the commander of our 11th armored division about 1943 before we left. It was a Clark and it was a Wesley Clark and this is a Wesley Clark. It's gotta be his son.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah, I would think so.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Because there was a Mark E. Clark, but he was in --

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, Mark Clark was down in Italy.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: The first armor.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, first armor. He was down in Italy and come up through Italy and was good. Yeah, General Mark Clark.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: I went to his NCL school.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, you did? Oh. Oh, he had a good reputation. Mark Clark. That's good. Yeah. Oh. Where did they hold that school at?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Fort Hood, Texas.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Oh, they did?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Mm-Hmm.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah, Mark Clark.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: So we'd like to say it was very interesting.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well, like I say, I was no big hero, I just did my duty, went through and did the best I could. Yeah, I just, you know, well if you do the best you can and do your job that's all they ask of you, you know? The best thing. Don't give 'em any problems. And you get promoted and you go up and it's not too bad. If you fight the problem, you're gonna lose. The Army's gonna win.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Keep your head down and keep your mouth shut.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: That's what they told me.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Don't look for trouble, because you're sure gonna find it.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: (Laughter) __.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: That's right. Yeah. I ended up with a good rank though, I tell ya that.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah, I'd say.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: I can go to the NCO club. I can go to the Alter's (PH) Club. I'm like a politician. I'm independent. I can go anyway. Then you feel at home in both clubs, you know?

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Mm-Hmm.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Yeah. So I hope this helps and you can use some of it and it helps you out with your class.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: It did.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Cause I had a class I took -- I come back and I want to college nights. Cause I was in -- I went back over to France after the war. I couldn't get assigned to Germany. I got married and I went overseas with the Army in between tours after that. Couldn't get to Germany and went to France and went to the University of Verdun at what was called the William and Mary branch at Verdun. I got two years training there. I got my French and my math and my English all in two years. I got a two year credit. Came back here and went to Saint Leo. Got my other two out of four. All on Army paid for. All I do is give 'em time. Two nights a week, from six to ten every night, two nights a week. So you get an education, too.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah. That wasn't bad.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: So I end up with four years on the Army. Didn't hurt my resume. Didn't hurt me any. I might of found out how dumb I was. That's really what would to me. Keeps you going. The more you go, the more you say, gee, I didn't know that. I can know this. And it keeps you motivated. And there's still a helluva a lot to learn. It's just a matter of -- that's why you get tired of sitting in school. You gotta get out and make a living, too.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah. You gotta get out and make some money.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Well, thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Well, I hope you can use it and help you out.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Cause I know, I had to interview -- what was it for? Some course I had to interview somebody. Just like you did. I can -- I can -- this was back in 1978-79. That's when I was working. I had to go interview somebody on public relations or something, just like you did. So you know I'm say I'm never too old, I can still learn. I am glad I could help you out a little, anyhow. Hope it does good.

sp.speaker: Candice Nunnally
sp.p: Yeah. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Malcolm McDonald
sp.p: Mm-Hmm. Good. Where do you live?
